description: A world tour of ancient peoples written for 8–12 year olds by Wikijunior volunteers, from the Sumerians and Egyptians to the Vikings, the Maya, and the Inca. Every page answers the same questions: where they lived, what they built, ate, wore, believed and wrote, and what is left of them today. Each day you read one page together, find the place on a map, and add a page to a notebook and a timeline. It's a free, openly licensed book; every page is free to read on Wikibooks.
includes: Link to the free Wikibooks page for every lesson
A notebook page and timeline entry for each civilization
Map work for every people you meet
Questions with answers for every lesson

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Once Upon a Time
steps: Read the introduction together
Start a long paper timeline across a wall or hallway
Narrate the order of the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages
questions: Which came first: the Bronze Age or the Stone Age?

lessons.title: Lesson 2: What Is a Civilization?
steps: Read the page together
Talk about what a group of people needs to count as a civilization
List three things our own civilization passes on to the next generation
questions: What Latin word meaning 'citizen' is the word civilization related to?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Archaeology
steps: Read the page together
Bury a few objects in layers in a tub of sand and dig them up like an archaeologist
Narrate how layers in the ground help date a find
questions: What do we call objects that archaeologists dig up?
What modern method uses carbon-14 to tell how old something is?

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Prehistory
steps: Read the page together
Draw a cave painting with chalk or charcoal
Narrate how people remembered things before writing
questions: What does 'prehistory' mean?
About how long ago was writing invented?

units.title: Unit 2: Mesopotamia and the Near East

Read the page together
Press wedge marks into clay with a craft stick to try cuneiform
questions: What were the Sumerians the first to invent?
Who is the most famous Sumerian?
Name one Sumerian invention still used today.

lessons.title: Lesson 18: The Romans, Part 1

Find Rome and the lands of its empire on a world map and add it to your timeline
Add a notebook page: where they lived, how they wrote, what they left behind
questions: What alphabet did the Romans develop?
What does polytheistic mean?

lessons.title: Lesson 19: The Romans, Part 2
steps: Read the sections on everyday life: beauty, marriage, slaves, children, and shows
Talk about how a Roman child's life differed from yours
Narrate what you would and would not have liked about Roman life
questions: How did the Romans get most of their slaves?
About how many days a year were taken up by Roman shows in the 300s?
answers: From prisoners of war and conquered cities
lessons.notes: These sections discuss marriage and slavery frankly; read them yourself first and choose what to share.
